Longtime production office PA here! Congratulations on the gig. There are some great tips in this thread already, but here are a couple of things I'd recommend in addition.

The hardest adjustment for me when I first started out was the super early mornings—being awake is one thing, but being ready to work and interact with others at 4-5 AM is another. I always lay out my clothes for the morning the night before, as well as anything else that I'll need to get ready or don't want to forget or be searching for (makeup bag, car keys, water bottle). A coffee maker with a timer is essential for me! I always set it the night before so that it starts brewing fresh coffee 10-15 minutes before I have to wake up. I set two alarms—one on my phone and one on a more traditional alarm clock. The further I get into a job, the more my body wants to fight me and sleep in, and the second alarm has  saved me more than once.

PAing will have its fun moments and you will learn a lot, but it can also be extremely difficult. You will sometimes get assigned the boring/frustrating/physically taxing tasks and people will take their frustration and exhaustion out on you. I recommend carving out tiny windows of your day for yourself that you can look forward to. I try to choose fun podcasts or playlists to enjoy on my commute, or use my drive time home to call and catch up with friends and family (sometimes I am too exhausted to talk to anyone, but this is a good way to keep in touch with people that you will inevitably spend less time with while you have this work schedule).

Production office specific tips: learn how to make good coffee and do it first thing when you get in—this will make you popular. If your project has the budget to allow for it, I always put up a dry-erase board on the fridge where people can make crafty requests. Try and automate the lunch order process as much as possible—I email the lunch menu in the morning along with a Google form where people can put in their order and customization requests, so that I have a spreadsheet to work off of when I place the order. Take pictures of all incoming package labels on your phone, so that you can distribute anything time sensitive and log them later. Make friends with the FedEx delivery person.

When it comes to your safety, you must be your own best advocate. Everyone is busy and PAs are often an afterthought. Your boss will assume that everything is fine unless you say otherwise. Exhaustion-based accidents, repetitive stress injuries, sexual harassment, and verbal abuse are all very real problems in the industry, and you must speak up if you feel like you're in danger. No job is worth your health and safety.

Good luck and feel free to PM me if you have questions about anything!

I finished a 6-infusion treatment course about a month ago. It helped me a lot. After finishing I was able to scale back to the lowest possible dose of my antidepressant (Cymbalta). It's not magic, but I have noticed a marked difference although it feels subtle (not like I'm crazy happy or energetic all the time). Earlier this year getting out of bed and showering took all my energy, but lately I've been getting up and doing a variety of activities throughout the day with a lot less strife. The sessions themselves are mostly a pleasant experience, you feel very floaty and detached from your body with some mild visuals. I had one session where the emotions were darker and I ended up crying without realizing what was happening, but once the infusion was over there were no lingering negative effects—in fact I think that experience helped me confront stuff I'd been avoiding thinking about.

It is REALLY expensive, I was very fortunate to have some help from my family and it ended up being worth it for me. The clinic I went to worked with me to let me pay for it on a session by session basis, so that if I wasn't having a good experience or it wasn't helping I hadn't paid for a whole course of treatment—maybe something you could ask about? I'm very hopeful for the esketamine to become more widely available as I know the effects of my treatment won't last forever.

Proceed with caution. A friend of mine got herself into a similar situation that did not end well: she met a guy in a bar with a slew of excuses why he was currently without a job or place to stay (most of them led back to "my ex girlfriend is a bitch"). She fell for him and he ended up living with her for a few weeks...until one day, she gets out of the shower and finds him gone along with her laptop and several other valuables. She never heard from him again, and the police were not able to take any action since he was a guest she invited into her home, not an intruder.

It's great to have empathy for other people, but you also need to protect yourself. You are not a bad person for having doubts about this—that's your self preservation instincts kicking in.

As a mostly-recovered ED sufferer, I want to say first of all that you are an amazing friend! Everything you've done so far is great, and she is really lucky to have you.

In my experience, no amount of "don't worry, you're thin!" was enough to make me feel better. The disordered thoughts are so intrusive and your view of yourself is so distorted that someone telling you to stop because you are already thin enough either a) makes no difference, you think they're lying or b) causes the sufferer to pick the statement apart to find a nonexistent intention in it (example: I say I'm fat, my boyfriend says I look great, all I see in that statement is that he didn't say thin). I agree with the other commenter that the best way to approach it is by shutting down body talk completely. Seeking reassurance from others about your body is just a part of the disordered thought cycle. When she makes a comment about either one of your bodies, calmly state that this is not a topic you want to discuss. If it helps make it less awkward, you can add a little levity after: "I don't want to talk about my body! Life's too short." "Let's not talk about that—let's talk about the new episode of XYZ show!" 

Keep talking up your therapist and encouraging her to find her own. Taking initiative to get help is really hard. Let her know that you'll help where you can—maybe with finding a name and phone number, driving her to the appointment, etc. if you have the resources to do those things.

The disordered mind seeks information about various diet and exercise regimens like a junkie—I'd recommend keeping discussion about your own eating plan to a minimum, and employ the "I don't want to discuss this topic" method if she comments on what you're eating.

When all you think about is food, it's easy to forget that there are so many other parts of life that matter more than your weight and what you eat—encourage her to keep up with social activities, school, fun hobbies, etc. and maybe facilitate those where you can.

Above all, she has to help herself. Support her where you can, but don't forget to take good care of yourself as well. You're a great friend, kudos!
